newsitem.title: USA: As election nears, Clinton campaigns for others.
newsitem.headline: As election nears, Clinton campaigns for others.

text.p: With a strong lead over Republican Bob Dole, U.S. President Bill Clinton began a four-day, five-state campaign trip on Sunday designed to help Democratic candidates for Congress as much as his own re-election effort.

Leading Dole by double digits in most opinion polls only 16 days from the Nov. 5 election, Clinton aides said the president was increasingly devoting his time and energy to trying to win back the Republican-controlled Congress.
Sunday was a case in point.
Clinton began his day by praying with U.S. Senate candidate Bob Torricelli at the New Hope Baptist Church in Newark, New Jersey, and exhorting the mostly black congregation to vote.

After church, Clinton drummed up about $800,000 in campaign contributions in Teaneck, New Jersey, for Torricelli, who is running neck-and-neck with Republican Richard Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by retiring Democrat Bill Bradley.
Speaking with Torricelli and New Jersey Democratic Sen. Frank Lautenberg beside him, the president sought to paint the Republicans as ruthless in their proposed budget cuts.

"With the support of Senator Lautenberg and Congressman Torricelli, we reduced the size of the bureaucracy, the number of regulations, more than the two previous administrations," Clinton told the donors.
"But we felt that we still had some responsibilities ... which included protecting the environment, giving people the chance to get an education, investing in our common economic future," he added.
Clinton's speech was briefly interrupted by a heckler from the Workers' World Party who criticised his foreign policy, notably on Iraq, prompting a tart response from the president.

"We have not killed a million people with our blockade of Iraq," he said. "(Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein could have had food and medicine for his children three years ago and he refused to take it."

Clinton was to attend four more fundraisers for Democratic candidates later in the day in New York state, expected to raise roughly $3 million to $4 million, and at least one fundraiser each in Ohio, Michigan and Florida as he campaigns over the next three days.
"We're going to do what it takes to win them all and we are trying ... to help not only ourselves, but our friends," White House political director Doug Sosnik said in an interview.
Clinton's fundraising coincided with growing criticism from Republicans of his campaign's having accepted $425,000 from an Indonesian couple with ties to the Lippo Group conglomerate of Indonesia.
White House chief of staff Leon Panetta dismissed the Republican attack as hypocrisy and said it was a negative campaign tactic that was not helping Dole.

"What he is doing is a negative attack on the president and it is not working," Panetta said on NBC's Meet the Press show. "There is hypocrisy here," he added, claiming the Republicans also accepted campaign contributions from foreign backers.
"Both sides do it," he said. "There is nothing that has been done that is wrong."
On the current, four-day swing, Clinton will make campaign stops in five states that have 112 of the 270 electoral college votes needed to win the presidency.
Sosnik described many of the appearances as "two-fers, if not three-fers," meaning they were designed to help Clinton, Democratic Senate candidates and others down the ticket.
Clinton has already devoted much time this year to helping Torricelli, who is locked in a tight race with Republican Zimmer, by raising cash and making joint campaign appearances.
The Torricelli-Zimmer race has been viewed as a toss-up for months although one poll, published on Oct. 15 in the Asbury Park Press, showed Torricelli beating Zimmer by 38 percent to 32 percent.
But a sizable 24 percent said they were still undecided, and the poll carries a 3.8 percent margin of error.
Later in the week Clinton was due to travel to three states with Senate races this year -- Alabama, Georgia and Louisiana -- whose contests were particularly hard fought.
